stories.title: ANALYSIS: Does Nets’ closing problem have solution?
stories.summary: With close losses continuing to pile up, the Nets’ late-game struggles have been on full display this year.
stories.detailText: NEW YORK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 18: Head coach, Jordi Fernandez of the Brooklyn Nets reacts during the first quarter against the Chicago Bulls at Barclays Center on November 18, 2026 in New York City. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images The idea of having the best of both worlds sounds nice, right? Unfortunately, in life, things typically don’t work that way. There are trade-offs in just about everything. The frustrating part is that either choice feels wrong, especially in the NBA. But neither choice is exactly right, either. It’s an interesting conundrum, especially if you are the 2026-27 Brooklyn Nets. Through 15 games, Brooklyn, sitting at 3-12, has somehow managed to lose five games by 15+ points. It’s the most in the league. However, the squad has also dropped four games by five points or fewer. That’s what makes the Nets’ start to the season so interesting. There have certainly been several blowouts, and the squad has only three wins, but there is also a chunk of games where Brooklyn was in it until the final buzzer. That includes Friday’s tough 113-111 loss to the Orlando Magic. According to Cleaning the Glass, Brooklyn has won 1.4 fewer games than their point differential would suggest, the fifth-worst mark in the league. Based on their -7.1 point differential, the Nets would be expected to have 4.4 wins through 15 games. When those games get tight, the Nets just haven’t been able to pull away consistently. Despite having the NBA’s highest effective field goal percentage in the fourth quarter, their shooting drops off significantly in clutch situations — the final few minutes of games. The Nets are shooting just 37.2% from the field in those moments, ranking 23rd in the league. Their free-throw shooting has been even worse, sitting at 60%, the fourth-worst mark. Subsequently, the Nets’ winning percentage in clutch situations is just 20.0%, the third-lowest clip in the NBA. The biggest problem comes with closing games, not necessarily being competitive or keeping it close entering the fourth. Is it coaching? Is it execution? Is it the lack of a closer? The Nets seem to be searching for those same answers themselves. However, from afar, Jordi Fernández looks to be facing a deeper problem that could be out of control. There is only so much he can do with his rotations. Even on Friday night, he switched up a multitude of components in his minutes distribution, including starting Danny Wolf over Egor Dëmin, which ultimately panned out. In large part, the overarching issue with Brooklyn comes back to the trade-off element. Want more scoring? There’s a good chance you’re sacrificing defense. Prioritize the other end? You probably have to sacrifice scoring. Fernández isn’t entirely absolved of blame, but the Nets lack legitimate two-way players. And when you’re trying to win a game in the final minutes, particularly against more talented teams, that only makes it harder. Compromise city The Nets have been stuck in a tough predicament, trying to balance what matters most in late-game situations: offense or defense. That has cost them in multiple games. At the end of the day, the Nets don’t have an established closing lineup. And that’s hard to overcome in today’s NBA, especially when games slow down in the final few minutes, and there’s little margin for error. Think about some of the better teams in the league, some that Brooklyn has even played. When a game gets tight, there is a pretty solid understanding of who’s getting the basketball. Most solid squads have that guy they trust in crucial situations to turn to when things start to break down. First off, who is that guy for the Nets? Michael Porter Jr. is probably the closest thing. He has been their most dependable offensive weapon, but is he really that high-end takeover guy? That’s where the roster’s lack of two-way versatility becomes even more problematic. When Fernández needs offense, he has to consider which players give Brooklyn the best chance to score. However, in many cases, that comes at the expense of defense. That’s what’s so frustrating with the state of the roster. Unfortunately for the Nets, it’s not as simple as just putting “the five best players” out on the court. It’s simply not how the roster is constructed: eight players are on rookie contracts, and the team is the second-youngest in the NBA over the past 25 years, older than only last year’s group. The Nets lack a proven guy who can dominate games down the stretch. Obviously that comes over time, and for a rebuilding team like Brooklyn, a player like that doesn’t emerge overnight. The hope is that Mikel Brown Jr. can become that guy, and the early returns on the rookie are promising so far, but he is still just 12 games into his NBA career while also being on a minutes restriction. Individually, Brooklyn has pieces that can be useful. It’s been promising to see growth from players like Nolan Traoré and Danny Wolf, looking to take legitimate second-year leaps. Julius Randle and MPJ add veteran experience and scoring punch. Then there is someone like Day’Ron Sharpe who has impressed while emerging as the team’s starting big. Those players can be useful. Collectively, though, it’s tough to find a five-man combination that doesn’t leave something to be desired. For a young team, there is some encouragement in being competitive. Hanging with high-level teams down the stretch like the Boston Celtics and the New York Knicks is encouraging, but when will those tight games actually translate into wins? There is also a distinction between being competitive but losing and losing games that are supposed to be wins, especially against strong competition. The latter can’t always be used as an excuse. What about Jordi? The head coach isn’t completely out of this conversation. A few of his rotational decisions, even with the newer changes, have been questionable. Look no further than Noah Clowney. Clowney, 22, is in the final year of his rookie contract. While he’s still 22, he hasn’t produced much consistently. That’s been the biggest concern with the Alabama product since he entered the league. Through 15 games, though, he hasn’t done much to change that narrative. In 21 minutes per game, he is averaging 6.5 points, 4.2 rebounds, and 1.1 assists on 41.3% from the field. Furthermore, he owns a team-low -107 plus/minus. For context, that’s also a 17-percentage-point difference between him and the second-lowest-rated net: Mo Wagner at -90. Meanwhile, his 3-point percentage (27.7%) is also the lowest on the team among qualified shooters (minimum 3.0 attempts per game). There have been some glimpses. He had back-to-back games against Memphis and New Orleans where he finished with at least 15 points and two 3s. Overall, though, not much has changed. The flashes are still there, but Clowney continues to struggle to find that level of consistency. And that brings us back to Friday night, when he finished with zero points in 22 minutes, shooting 0-of-4 from the field, and recording a team-worst minus-12 rating. Yet, with the game on the line, he was still on the floor, defending Franz Wagner, who hit the game-winning shot over him. Now Wagner had a tremendous game, finishing with 35 points, and his offensive ability is highly touted. However, putting Clowney out there in that situation was questionable to begin with. If he isn’t providing offensively, what exactly is the team gaining by keeping him out there? While he came away with a block and a steal, he hasn’t been regarded as a plus defender, especially for his position and size, at 6’10” and 210 pounds. Most glaringly, his plus/minus rating was not only the lowest on Friday, but it’s also the lowest among the whole team this year, and by a pretty wide margin. Despite that, though, he continues to earn consistent minutes. He ranks eighth on the team in minutes per game (21.0), behind Randle (33.1), Porter (32.9), Dëmin (24.0), Sharpe (23.9), Wolf (23.0), Brown (22.9), and Traoré (22.3). So esentially, he’s been the Nets’ third player off the bench this season. That’s a pretty important role. Clearly, with him in that role and out on the court to close games, things haven’t been working too well. That’s where Fernández comes in. He needs to be willing to make more on-the-fly adjustments to the rotation, especially when things aren’t working. How about looking at players like Josh Minott and Drake Powell? Neither has received notable minutes this season out of garbage time. Neither is a proven NBA defender, but is it time to give them minutes to see what happens? It’s worked with Danny Wolf. After all, isn’t that supposed to be part of a rebuilding season? Minott, 23, shot 39.5% from deep wth Brooklyn last year after being acquired at the trade deadline, and the organization saw enough to award him a two-year, $9 million extension in the offseason. At 6’8” and 205 pounds, he also has the tools to be a disruptor on the defensive end. Powell, meanwhile, has spent much of the season in the G League so far with Brooklyn’s affiliate, the Long Island Nets. He has played in five NBA games and was called up for Friday, although most of his minutes have come in garbage time. The North Carolina product boasts a 43-inch vertical and a 7-foot wingspan, giving him intriguing potential on offense and defense, notably at the point of attack. That was on display at points last year. In fact, his 91.9 defensive rating led the NBA last December, and the Nets actually went 7-4 that month. Of course, the Nets have a free agency decision on Clowney coming up in the Summer. And of course, the Nets are bringing Powell along slowly. He was, after all, the biggest reach of the Flatbush 5. But, of course, the offense remains a work in progress. He shot just 28% from 3 during his rookie campaign and a painful 4-of-16 from that range in Summer League, including a 0-of-14 start. There is also two-way forward Chaney Johnson, who played a firm role in the rotation at the start of the season, but his minutes have gradually disappeared. Johnson still lacks an established offensive game, but he can guard multiple positions on both ends of the floor. Maybe Minott struggles. Maybe Powell shows that he isn’t ready. Maybe Johnson doesn’t improve much either. However, getting that understanding is important, especially when things aren’t working. And if one of them does emerge as a useful piece, particularly defensively, that would be huge for the roster’s current outlook. There may not be a perfect solution. At 3-12, though, the team needs to keep experimenting, especially off the bench. Fernández’ decision regarding Dëmin and Wolf on Friday paid off; now it’s important to see that same mindset carry over to bench minutes. Given the organization’s overall situation, there’s much more to gain from trying something different than sticking with what hasn’t worked.

stories.title: Rockets must choose carefully in strange 2027 NBA Draft
stories.summary: The Rockets could have two high picks, but ready made stars won’t be easy to find.
stories.detailText: TUCSON, AZ - NOVEMBER 18: Arizona Wildcats forward Ivan Kharchenkov (8) celebrates on the court during first half of a basketball game between the UConn Huskies and the Arizona Wildcats on November 18, 2026 at McKale Center at ALKEME Arena in Tucson, AZ. (Photo by Christopher Hook/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images If the 2026-27 NBA season ended today, the Houston Rockets would have roughly a 64% chance of landing a top-five pick. I thought it was roughly 80%. The Brooklyn Nets and Phoenix Suns both have 40%-ish odds; add them together, 40%. I was, as is so often the case, corrected on X. If each independent event has a 40% chance of happening, each has a 60% chance of not happening. So anyway, long and short, accounting for that, it’s about 64%. That’s pretty good. Remember when Rafael Stone said not to judge the James Harden trade until 2030? Well, we’re almost in 2027, and it feels pretty safe to credit Stone’s vision. The Rockets are 12-4; it’s nearly certain that they’ll have a lottery pick (and probably two) this summer, and there’s a pretty good chance one of those picks lands in the top five. Life is good. Only… Rockets’ luck comes at the wrong time There’s always a catch, isn’t there? The Rockets draft one of the best centers of all time in the same draft that the best player of all time is drafted in. They change NBA offense, but another team changes it even more. Whatever. The catch is that this draft is widely viewed as weak. If you’ve researched it, you’ve likely come to the same conclusion. There’s Kansas’ Tyran Stokes, and then…yeah. At least, the list of (nearly) surefire NBA stars begins and ends with Stokes. That doesn’t mean there aren’t quality players in the draft: It means Rafael Stone will have to dig for them. Caveat One: We’re early in the draft cycle. It’s entirely possible that someone whose name isn’t in the most thorough Excel file on the most obsessive aspiring internet scout’s laptop. Caveat Two: I wrote a whole piece about how the Rockets should be looking at Baba Oladotun, and he’s averaging a red-hot 4, 2, and 1. Have your grain of salt on hand. Rockets must dig deep for talent Right now, I’m fixated on two particular prospects. Illinois’ Quentin Coleman is a 6’4″ combo guard. I’m convinced he’s got a distinctly positive wingspan – I’d estimate 6’8″ – but Google has no idea. He’s averaging 17.8 points, 6.8 rebounds, and 4.4 assists while shooting 55.6% from the field and 37.0% from three-point range on 5.4 attempts per game. The cool thing about Coleman is that he’s a lead ball-handler who plays with the energy of a role player. He reminds me of a young Lonzo Ball, with maybe a bit more on-ball juice and a bit less defense. The other is Ivan Kharchenkov, a 6’7″, 230-pound wing on Arizona. Kharchenkov almost entered the draft last year. He’s an outstanding, aggressive perimeter defender with some ancillary skills: He can pass and dribble some. The problem with Kharchenkov has always been his low three-point volume, which never bodes well for an NBA role player. This year, Kharchenkov is forcing us to ask a question: What if he isn’t a role player? He’s averaging 22.6 points, 8.0 rebounds, and 4.6 assists per game. Those are not role player numbers. There are concerns about Kharchenkov. He’s still shooting just 4.0 threes per game. It’s also been suggested that his strength-based shot creation won’t work in the NBA, where men are stronger. If he’s forced to fend for himself, Kharchenkov tends to muscle into his defender with a few dribbles to create space for his mid-range. Those are my guys. You may have your own. The broader point is this: Very few “bad” NBA drafts are as bad as they were perceived to be in hindsight. It does happen, but more often, there are stars hiding in plain sight. At this convergence of fortune and strategy, all the Rockets can do is choose carefully. It could be the difference between finding the would-be best team in the NBA’s missing piece, and adding another dud to rot away in the 8th man spot until he’s trade fodder. For now, let’s wait and see what the Draft Gods decide.

stories.title: Mikal Bridges shakes off slump, hits buzzer-beater to save Knicks vs. Blazers
stories.summary: Mired in a shooting slump, Mikal Bridges delivered a buzzer-beating 3-pointer to lift the Knicks past the Trail Blazers after they squandered a 26-point lead.
stories.detailText: NEW YORK -- Mired in a shooting slump that has left him struggling to meet his standards, Mikal Bridges seemed like the most unlikely New York Knicks player to rescue them against the Portland Trail Blazers on Saturday night. But with Jalen Brunson blanketed in the closing seconds and the Knicks down two, Bridges found himself open off an inbounds pass from Josh Hart , set his feet behind the 3-point line and nailed a buzzer-beating 3-pointer to give New York a 97-96 win at Madison Square Garden. Bridges' shot, which came on a night the team honored alumni from all eras, saved the Knicks after they had squandered a 26-point lead. "How Josh threw it kind of indicated that I was going to be open, so you just try to make a play," said Bridges, who finished with 12 points on 5-of-8 shooting. "It's great, you know. First, you win the game, but second, seeing the joy of those guys, and obviously you know tonight with alumni and stuff, it's a pretty cool moment." The dramatic finish came after Knicks center Andre Drummond , starting in place of Karl-Anthony Towns (illness), fouled Blazers forward Deni Avdija 30 feet from the basket with 3.2 seconds left. Avdija's ensuing free throws gave Portland its first lead of the game. For Bridges, the game winner offered a welcome moment amid a difficult season. His shooting numbers have fallen to career lows, as have his minutes, with Knicks coach Mike Brown increasingly turning to other options late in games. Bridges, who has averaged 14.5 points on 48.4% shooting and 33.1 minutes per game in his career, is managing just 7.8 points on 41.8% shooting in 26.1 minutes this season. Although Bridges has remained a starter, Brown has opted to play veteran Landry Shamet late in games. Shamet has been one of the NBA's most potent 3-point shooters at 45.3% this season. But with Towns, OG Anunoby and Jordan Clarkson out, Brown needed Bridges on the floor. "He's the same," Brown said. "When quote-unquote, we think he's struggling, he just keeps playing and doesn't let anything impact him. He's going to let it fly, he's going to push it, and he's going to defend." Bridges' 12-point effort continued a recent trend in which he has played well every other night. Before Saturday, his scoring totals over the previous five games were eight, 17, five, 18 and two points. "But he's not going to get too high. He's not going to get too low," Brown said. "So for him to have the ball in his hands at that point in the game, there's a lot of confidence not only coming from him but from his teammates and the staff." Brunson, who led the Knicks with 30 points, missed all five of his fourth-quarter shots as New York nearly let a commanding lead slip away. The Knicks shot 5-of-22 in the period before Bridges bailed them out. "When you're continuously working on your game every single day, and things may not be falling in your favor, but you keep doing the right thing every single day, eventually things are going to turn for you," Brunson said. "Over the past week or two, things have been turning for him, and now he's on a roll." Bridges' up-and-down season has been emblematic of the uneven play of the Knicks, who sometimes have looked like two different teams within the same game. Early Saturday, it looked like an exhibition of style points, with the Knicks hitting their first eight attempts from the 3-point line. Even Drummond connected on his first triple of the year. But a 66-40 game right before halftime slowly turned. It was a familiar pattern for the Knicks, who also built a big lead Thursday night in Minnesota before struggling to prevail. "You give them credit, but in the same breath, you know that you can play better and you hope to play better," Brown said. "It was taking our foot off the gas, and we have to be better." Like the past legends who were honored at Madison Square Garden on Saturday night, Bridges will be a member of Knicks alumni one day, celebrated for what he helped the franchise accomplish in his career. His highlights will endure, and the details won't matter when he finds himself on the sideline as a retired Knick years down the line. In the moment, though, he wouldn't allow himself to reflect on his up-and-down journey this season, saying only: "It was a good win."

stories.title: Knicks 97, Trail Blazers 96: “We found a way to get a win”
stories.summary: A win is a win?
stories.detailText: NEW YORK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 21: Mikal Bridges #25 of the New York Knicks shoots the winning three point shot against Toumani Camara #33 of the Portland Trail Blazers during the fourth quarter at Madison Square Garden on November 21, 2026 in New York City. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images If you wanted to explain to a new sports fan what the term “tale of two halves” means, just show them the tape from last night. The game started with a classic Jalen Brunson takeover that saw him go for 19 points, four rebounds, and two assists while shooting 6-7 from the field and 5-5 from three. And the Knicks did an amazing job playing off of his confidence and gravity en route to 40 first-quarter points. New York was playing with pace; the ball movement and player movement were constant and crisp, and everybody got in on the action. For a moment or two, it was reminiscent of the Knicks’ Mother’s Day massacre of the 76ers in the playoffs just months ago. New York ended the first quarter with nine three-pointers while missing just two. Aside from Brunson’s aforementioned five made threes, Mikal Bridges, Andre Drummond, Shamet, and McBride all added one each. And besides the nine threes, the Knicks had two dunks and one mid-range jump shot by Brunson. It was one of the most analytically beautiful shot charts anyone has ever seen. The Trail Blazers, on the other hand, managed to score just 23 points in the first quarter. Deni Avdija did get off to a nice start with eight points, and Damian Lillard chipped in six of his own that accounted for more than half of their team’s points. Toumani Camara, who was Trail Blazers head coach Micah Nori’s answer to trying to stop Brunson, started off the game cold; Cidy Sissoko went scoreless, and starting center Donovan Clingan added just three points. Q: "Jalen Brunson…how do you plan to slow him down tonight?" Blazers coach Micah Nori: "Toumani Camara" pic.twitter.com/mS88qsFFdP — New York Basketball (@NBA_NewYork) November 22, 2026 The second quarter didn’t produce the same kind of exhilarating offense as the Knicks scored “just” 26 points. But even with the shooting seeing some expected negative regression, the Knicks still won the quarter by six as the Trail Blazers’ offense limped its way to a 20-point quarter. The Knicks did struggle a bit with Brunson out as a Kolek-led second unit got some quality looks but just could not create advantages on a consistent basis. But as Knicks fans have said plenty of times over the last couple of years, thank god for Shamet. The veteran guard came up huge throughout the entire game as Brunson’s much-needed sidekick. Shamet scored 13 of his 20 points in the second quarter and helped the Knicks take a 23-point lead into halftime. But as noted earlier, the second half looked like a completely different ball game. The Knicks played one of their worst offensive quarters of the season, managing to score just 15 total points. Some of that was the Trail Blazers amping up the defense and coming out playing much more energized and more physical. But as head coach Mike Brown alluded to after the game, the Knicks looked like they were stuck in mud. There was significantly less movement overall. The ball was no longer zipping around the perimeter. Players were stagnant. And they no longer had the shooting touch to mask their lackluster offensive execution and subpar process. The Trail Blazers offense scored 29 points in the period and just like that, the lead was cut down to just nine points. The Knicks often like to keep their fans on the edge of their seats, and Saturday night was no exception. Instead of dominating the third quarter with the same type of execution and intensity that they started the game with and taking the Trail Blazers out of the game, it was now down to one quarter. And you could tell early on in the final period that this wasn’t going to be an easy win for the Knicks to pull out. The Trail Blazers now had the confidence and the momentum. Lillard had struggled for much of the game, but he hit some key shots. Clingan was now dominating the paint and was on his way to a 22-point, 13-rebound double-double. Avdija, despite the Knicks generally playing good defense on him, was getting going. And that was happening all while the Knicks’ offensive struggles continued. The Trail Blazers continued their upped intensity and were doing a much better job sticking with Shamet. Brunson, who was starting to look fatigued, was missing shots he usually makes. And both of those things were made much worse by the fact that Josh Hart, who had done a lot of nice non-scoring things in the first half, wasn’t looking to shoot at all. But there’s a reason everyone calls the NBA a make-or-miss league. With the Trail Blazers taking a two-point lead in the final seconds thanks to a clutch three by Lillard, Bridges, who has slowly but surely turned the page on what was a disastrous first few weeks of the season, made a game-winning three against the Trail Blazers for the second time in three seasons. MIKAL BRIDGES HITS THE @TISSOT BUZZER-BEATER AS THE KNICKS WIN THEIR FOURTH STRAIGHT! 🚨⏰ Everyone Gets 24 pic.twitter.com/UmtE1mOLRu — NBA (@NBA) November 22, 2026 Had he missed that shot, Saturday night’s loss would have turned into the worst loss of the season. Yes, Karl-Anthony Towns and OG Anunoby were sidelined. But to lose that game at home after how the first half started would’ve been a gut-wrenching loss. Instead, Bridges makes the shot and the Knicks win by one, and it’s the Trail Blazers who are now on the wrong side of what was objectively a fun NBA game. Portland finds themselves regretting how they came out in the first half, and Avdija has to be thinking about the three free throws he missed in the fourth quarter. The Knicks’ Saturday night win over the Trail Blazers was emblematic of the Knicks as a whole. Sometimes, they look like one of the best offenses of all time. Sometimes, they can’t concoct anything better than a stagnant possession that leads to a Brunson isolation with seconds left. But as Brown said during his postgame presser, they “found a way to get a win”. Mike Brown after Knicks 97-96 buzzer-beating win over Blazers: "I apologized to my team. I wanted to make a defensive substitution…I did not do it quick enough [so] that Dame 3 was on me…Our group…beautiful basketball both ends first half…touched paint, make quick decision,… pic.twitter.com/iWx7QcXk8C — New York Basketball (@NBA_NewYork) November 22, 2026 As this team has proven time and time again, regardless of who is playing and who is out, regardless of who the opponent is, this team will find ways to stay in the game, and more often than not, they’ll come out on top. It isn’t always easy. It isn’t always pretty. But a win is a win.

stories.title: Joe Mazzulla downplays disastrous third straight loss: ‘We played well enough’
stories.summary: Boston delivered a basement-level performance despite facing the 14-loss Kings on two days of rest Saturday night.
stories.detailText: SACRAMENTO, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 21: Head coach Joe Mazzulla of the Boston Celtics looks on in the first quarter against the Sacramento Kings at Golden 1 Center on November 21, 2026 in Sacramento, California. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) | Getty Images For the third straight time, the Boston Celtics went out like a dud, collapsing against the two-win Sacramento Kings on Saturday night without Jayson Tatum, Derrick White and Mitchell Robinson. But head coach Joe Mazzulla was rather dismissive afterward. “I think we played well enough to win the game,” Mazzulla told reporters, per CLNS Media , after Boston’s 97-96, “and they made more shots than we did, and made a couple of more plays down the stretch. You take a look at the process of the game, we played well and lost. So that’s what you take from [it] and move on to tomorrow.” Mazzulla turned to Paul George and Payton Pritchard to lead the pack. They shared the floor with Sam Hauser, Hugo González and Neemias Queta in Boston’s starting lineup. Yet the team’s strongest and most efficient contribution didn’t come from any of them. It came from 39-year-old guard Mike Conley, who had made just four appearances for Boston entering the night, averaging eight minutes per game before receiving 18 minutes off the bench in Sacramento. Conley scored 19 points, converting his first six consecutive shot attempts, while adding four rebounds, three assists and two steals. From the looks of it, Conley had himself a heroic, game-saving performance in the works, good enough to get the Celtics back in the column. He was active, up to speed and turned back the clock to his vintage Memphis Grizzlies days, even though he sat on the bench for the entire first and third quarters. Nov 21, 2026; Sacramento, California, USA; Boston Celtics forward Paul George (13) reacts during the third quarter against the Sacramento Kings at Golden 1 Center. Mandatory Credit: Justine Willard-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Had it not been for Conley’s out-of-the-blue scoring outburst, the Kings might’ve run the Celtics out of the building. Mazzulla believed it too. “He kept us in it,” Mazzulla said. “Tried to finish the game with him as much as we could. Thought he was great on both ends of the floor and tonight’s the reason why you have a guy like that on your roster, and he gave us a chance to win tonight.” Conley stood tall as Boston’s lone bright spot, tying George for the team’s lead in scoring while finishing as Boston’s plus-minus leader (+17). The Celtics performed well below their standard, underscoring the impact Tatum’s absence had against a Kings team that leads the Western Conference in turnovers (17.5), boasts the NBA’s second-lowest-scoring offense (106.8 points) and had won just one of its first 15 games entering Saturday night. Without their superstar, the wheels fell off the wagon. In the third quarter, Mazzulla’s group got outscored 35-13 and went 0-for-13 from three. With back-to-back rest days, the underperformance was all the more inexcusable. Boston finished the night shooting 33.7 percent from the field, going 34-for-101. They shot 22.4 percent from 3-point range, going 13-for-58 and setting a franchise record for most misses (45) in a single game. At the free-throw line, they went 15-for-25, adding further fuel to the fire. George went 6-for-21, Pritchard went 4-for-17 and Baylor Scheierman shot 2-for-11. Coming off consecutive losses to the Orlando Magic and Denver Nuggets, this was their ugliest dud by far. In the fourth quarter, the Celtics traded baskets with Sacramento as the clock ticked down. Queta hit a go-ahead 3-pointer from the corner with 3:47 remaining, only for Kings rookie Darius Acuff Jr. to drain the equalizer, also from beyond the arc. George grabbed an offensive rebound and finished the putback layup with 49 seconds left. Acuff answered by drawing a foul and sinking both free throws at the other end. Pritchard sank a clutch fadeaway jumper to give Boston a 96-95 lead with 12 seconds remaining. Then the Celtics failed to protect the glass on the ensuing possession. Acuff challenged González off the inbound, drove past him and missed his right-handed layup. But Sacramento’s Keegan Murray leaped over Devin Carter to secure the offensive rebound and finish the putback , giving the Kings a 97-96 lead and leaving Boston with just five seconds for redemption. For the game, Pritchard was handed the ball against Murray but failed to create enough space for a clean look, capping an already miserable performance with a wasted opportunity. Pritchard finished with nine points and missed all eight of his 3-point attempts, which he owned up to. “It’s frustrating,” Pritchard told reporters . “I just got to play better. I gotta do more, so a lot of that is on me in the third quarter and stuff like that. So it’s my fault for that one.” Pritchard on the final possession: “Obviously didn’t get to a good enough spot, and [Murray] played good defense. But probably need to try to find a better look, though.” The Celtics have lost three consecutive regular-season games for the first time since opening last season with three straight defeats. They suffered their most humbling loss yet, deservedly getting served their lunch by arguably the worst team in the NBA. Still, Mazzulla felt differently. “I thought we competed at a high level through just a drought offensively where we couldn’t make shots,” Mazzulla said. “And again, you have to stick to the process of it. I thought we played well enough to win, and we just didn’t. They made a few more plays than we did.” Winning and playing “well enough” to win aren’t mutually exclusive. However, the Celtics didn’t meet the threshold necessary to leave Sacramento victorious. Their result was entirely warranted.

stories.title: Inside the Suns: Ryan Dunn, Koa Peat, a wake up call?
stories.summary: Your weekly Inside the Suns analysis straight from the BSotS community who live and breathe the team.
stories.detailText: Welcome to Inside the Suns, a deep down analysis of the current Phoenix Suns team in which the Fantable — a round table of Bright Siders — give their takes on the Suns’ latest issues and news. Fantable Questions of the Week Q1: What are your thoughts on the progress of Ryan Dunn this season? GuarGuar: I’ve been really impressed with Ryan so far this season. He’s showing more control and poise in his game. He’s not recklessly driving at 100 mph to the rim every time he touches the ball. The jump shot mechanics look better, and he’s been impressive as a roll man this year. He’s been a pleasant surprise. zenzino: I love it! How could I not? As I wrote in a previous Fantable (or thread, I can’t remember), Dunn was considered by many (including me) to be the odd man out for rotational minutes this season. However, he became the poster child for the fact that progress is not linear. After a sophomore year where the improvement was slight (especially alongside Oso’s improvement), Dunn has made a leap in his third year. We never questioned his defense. He reportedly put in a lot of work on his shot this off-season. As he said himself, he ‘has to trust in the work’. This becomes evident during a game. When he has time to think about it, he’ll either pass up a shot or look more like last year’s shooting. When he doesn’t have time to think, his shot looks really good and goes in more often than not. The more he works, and the less time he has to think, the shots will go down, and he’ll gain enough confidence to think and shoot. This is also a lesson not to give up on Sheer. He may have a sophomore slump this season, but that doesn’t mean he’s not working and could come out later in the season or his third year to make a Dunn-like leap. Ashton: I am a little curious why Dunn’s minutes seem to vary by game. He is clearly the next man up at the power forward position. But, thus far, I have not paid enough attention to Dunn on the Fantable and he is impressing me as a future breakout candidate to start. So, my bad on not giving Ryan Dunn more love early. Also, Brooks said he would be willing to play bench minutes? Jaw hits the floor as he is coming off one of his best games against the Sacramento Kings. He stated that is to work on his playmaking with the better spacing that the bench provides. I applaud his heroic statement, but I am calling BS. The real reason is so he can terrorize opposing bench unit defenses into therapy with his constant chirping. Still, an intriguing thought to consider. Does Ott buy-in? I doubt it. That would make Ryan Dunn the starter for minutes if that were to come true. Some of the Suns’ lineups would be rife for consideration in the comment sections. OldAz: Personally, I love what Ryan has done this year. He has taken advantage of the lowered expectations, especially compared to last season when he was expected to come in and capture a larger role only to struggle with the new system and get stuck behind a number of veteran guards. This season, most had written him off coming into the season and were fine throwing him into whatever trade would accomplish moving whatever core player that fan wanted to move. Instead, he ratcheted up his defensive intensity and the speed at which he plays and has made a significant impact. My only complaint is with the coaching staff that seems to have way too long of a leash for veteran players to play emotionless, effortless basketball and only give a player like Ryan a few minutes despite their obvious positive impact on the overall result on the floor. Ryan is not going to fill up the stat sheet, but he is going to hustle on defense, compete for rebounds, and is willing to shoot or drive when he is left open. He is a perfect complement to Booker or any of the other “star” players on the court when Ott chooses to play him. He is one of those players (along with Goodwin, Gillespie, and Kennard) that you can pair with either center and 2 of the core starters and get a pretty decent lineup because of their hustle and energy. The only difference is he is the only one of those 4 that also brings some length to the court. I’m not overly worried about the recent little injuries, as I believe he has figured out that his energy and effort mean more than the stats he puts up each night. Hopefully Ott is starting to figure out the same thing. Rod: I hated to see him get hurt in the Jazz game. Hopefully. he won’t be out long because he’s become an important part of the Suns’ rotation. His offensive impact hasn’t been great, but he’s been playing more under control on that end and making positive contributions, both inside (5th most dunks on the team in just the 10th most minutes per game) and outside (42.3% from three). His biggest areas of impact have been on defense and in rebounding (per 36, he’s tied with Bridges for 2nd at 8.6). I’ll admit that I was one of the people who was almost ready to give up on Ryan this season if he didn’t show some improvement. Happily, he’s come through for us and is playing very well and under control. Q2: Was getting benched for the entire 4th quarter of the Lakers game a “wake up call” for the team’s starters? GuarGuar: I really hope it was a wake-up call. This starting lineup has been awful together, and the metrics don’t lie. The Jalen Green PG experiment has been an abject failure, and the sooner we move off of it, the better we will be. The bench plays together as a unit and with a ton of energy, the complete opposite of our starting unit. zenzino: I guess? How many wake-up calls do they need? They supposedly had one in the first game of the season. The first game! Maybe that benching did it, though. They definitely looked better against Denver and really came out against the Kings with aggressiveness, energy, and surprisingly good ball movement. It was the Kings, but maybe playing a few easier games in a row (Jazz & Pels next) will allow them to get some confidence/momentum. Recent reports amidst all the trade rumors/ideas say that the Suns are not shopping Green. They like the roster they have and are content to give these guys time to gel. I don’t know if it has anything to do with the benching, but we’re definitely seeing some improvement. It occurred to me the other day that it is the fans’ job to (over)react from game to game and the coaches/FO’s job NOT to react from game to game. Ashton: I hate this question. Beat LA, Beat LA! The fact of the matter is that the Lakers are that good. It was a nice salve to the wounds to see the Suns beat a good Nuggets team the day after. Which is exactly what the Suns need: beating the teams they are supposed to beat, but picking up a few wins against the teams that are not (Houston and Denver). The Lakers were not on the bingo card in the W category. Still, Ott probably wisely threw in the towel against a very good Lakers squad and allowed his starters to watch real basketball from the sidelines without getting injured. I was fine with it from a strategic point of view, but I am not fine with it from a fan point of view. Suns will get them next time! OldAz: Maybe. It certainly couldn’t have hurt as we have seen a better version of Brooks and Green since then, with more focus on the defensive end and moving the ball on offense instead of always forcing their own shots. I think Booker and Bridges were already playing well, but it really requires all the starters to be on the same page for that group to succeed. The better play and effort from all has also allowed Ott to play a little more randomly with lineups. Now the question is if the recent successes are more about this improved play and more diverse lineup combinations, or just a product of playing lesser teams that the Suns should handle like the Kings and Jazz. Rod: You could call it that, or you could call it a message from Ott, “Play with some heart or you’ll sit and watch your teammates show you what that means.” Whatever you want to call it, it seems to have worked in the games since then. You can have all the talent in the world, but without effort, players are just wasting the fans’ time (and patience) when they’re just going through the motions. I don’t want to see the starters playing like that again, and hopefully they got that message from Ott loud and clear…and won’t forget it. Q3: Does Koa Peat look ready for more rotation minutes, and who do you think loses court time to give them to him? GuarGuar: Koa is probably only useful as a small-ball 5 right now until he develops a jump shot, which looks to be a ways away. He has good instincts and can finish through contact pretty well, but he’s not close to being ready for a consistent rotation spot in my opinion. Next year will probably be a different discussion. zenzino: I think it’s pretty telling that he has spent zero time with the Valley Suns. My wild speculation is that Ott wants him with the team and ready to play. After looking great in quality minutes against the Lakers, Ott teased us with a 2nd-quarter appearance of Peat against the Nuggets. That lasted a minute. Literally. The next time we saw him was garbage time against the hapless Kings. When this question was first sent to us at the beginning of the week, my answer was that Koa should definitely get some Brooks minutes. Or even some Bridges minutes. But mostly Brooks. Up through the Lakers game, Brooks has been a shell of what we loved about him last season. Maybe, like cutting Sampson’s hair (and Dillon’s hair), Dillon’s effort to not get techs this season has stripped him of his strength. He was better against the Nuggets (got a tech) and was on fire against the Kings (no tech). Hopefully, he has turned a corner and will continue with the aggressive Villain we know and love. Techs and all. Bridges is showing progress with every game, and we are beginning to see what the FO envisioned with this addition. 14 games is not even close to enough games for a starter to fully integrate. As I said, the FO has to take the long view and not overreact game to game. So, barring injuries or a slide by either Brooks or Bridges, we will probably only see Koa in very specific matchup situations or garbage time. That’s ok for now. There’s a lot to learn from just being with the team. Especially if they continue the winning trend. Ashton: How to answer this one? Peat’s best game came against the Lakers. At least the Arizona guy gets it. But in the end, stats do not lie on small sample sizes. I am stealing a copy and paste from Hoops Nightly : Peat has appeared in 8 games and averages 4.5 minutes, 3.1 points, 0.9 rebounds and 0.1 assists. He is shooting 64.7 percent from the field and 100.0 percent at the line, with a 0.0 mark from three. His true shooting is 68.2 percent and his usage is 21.1. The plus-minus is 3.8. These numbers come from very few minutes, so they say little yet. His minutes have ranged from 1.3 to 8.2 in a night, and he has not scored in three of the eight games. Okay, with that out of the way (I hate talking stats – leave that to the board members), the stats still suggest that Peat’s minutes should increase if only to increase the sample size. And consistent minutes would probably help rather than 8 minutes here and a throw-in one minute there. Since the question asked if he “looks” ready for more rotational minutes, I would state an emphatic yes until proven otherwise. OldAz: In small doses, certainly. Just like we saw in the Jazz game, he needs to learn to play at this level without fouling, but that isn’t going to happen at the G League level or during garbage minutes when the refs also just want to get the game over. I think he should get about the same 5-6 minutes Dunn was getting earlier in the season, and given an opportunity to play more as he does well. To me, these minutes should be coming from Brooks, Green, Bridges, and even Booker, as up until the last few games the bench minutes have been better anyway, so Ott might as well mix and match more minutes with just 2 of those core 4 on the floor with a center and 2 bench players. Go ahead and compress the starters’ minutes while this is working, save more strain on the starters’ legs until later in the season and see who actually develops. I know this will never happen, but the Suns really have to come up with a better way to give minutes to young players at the NBA level and start developing them faster than they have been. Rod: Peat does look ready for more playing time, but for now, I think most of that time will come when Ott decides to play a small-ball lineup, so I don’t think he’ll be taking minutes away from anyone specifically. I’ve seen Ott try various players out in that role, and Koa just seems to be the best fit in that role. And considering the guy’s built like a linebacker, I’m not at all certain that we should even call it “small” ball when he’s at the 5. The three quick fouls he got in the Jazz game don’t change my mind. He may not be ready for a full-blown rotation spot, but he’s ready for spot rotation minutes. As always, many thanks to our Fantable members for all their extra effort this week! Quotes of the Week “You can see his (Jalen Green’s) speed. Anytime he’s in open court, anytime he gets downhill, that’s what we need. We need paint pressure. We’re a predominantly jump-shooting team. Him and Miles (Bridges) provide some of that paint pressure, that downhill thrust that we need offensively.” – Jordan Ott “We’re just gonna continue to talk about just stacking our small segments of time and that will build continually over time. We’ll get better. We believe in that. We believe every time we’re together, whether that’s a meal, whether that’s a shootaround, whether that’s a film session, that we have to go all in, all in, all the time, and they’ll continually stack.” – Jordan Ott “Collectively, we were in it for the full 48.” – Jordan Ott “I see Man-Man working every day. He’s one of the hardest workers I’ve ever played with.” – Miles Bridges “We have guys that want to win, that want to play the right way.” – Luke Kennard Suns Trivia/History On November 23, 1972, Charlie Scott recorded the Phoenix Suns’ first-ever triple-double with 42 points, 10 rebounds, and 15 assists in a 128-122 victory over the Detroit Pistons on Thanksgiving Day. On November 23, 1994, Wesley Person hit for 19 points to lead 10 double-figure scorers in Phoenix’s 140-109 home win over the LA Clippers. The Suns became the third team in NBA history to have 10 different players score in double figures in the same game. No Suns player shot less than 50% from the field that day, and the team FG percentage was 64.7% while also hitting 47.1% of their three-point attempts. On November 23, 2015, Devin Booker got his first career start for the Phoenix Suns, filling in for an injured Eric Bledsoe. Booker had 4 points, 1 assist, 4 rebounds, and 1 steal in his debut in the Suns’ starting lineup as Phoenix fell to the San Antonio Spurs 98-84. On November 24, 1989, the Suns reserves were outscored 16-0 to start the 4th quarter, so “only” up 28 points, head coach Cotton Fitzsimmons brought back his starters, allowing Jeff Hornacek to record the first triple-double of his career (22pts, 12 rebs, 15assists) in a 121-94 win over the Orlando Magic. On November 25, 1995, down 110-100 with 90 seconds left, the Suns nailed 4 three-pointers and, after Nick Van Exel inexplicably allowed himself to be tied up with 6.7 seconds left, Michael Finley hit a buzzer-beater to defeat the LA Lakers, 114-113. teamStories.detailText: Today I’m going to do something I don’t usually do here. I’m going to complain. And it’s a crazy feeling, complaining about a win like last night’s. It just doesn’t sit right. And, in a way, it feels oddly ungrateful. Hypocritical, even. Especially when you’ve spent a not-insignificant amount of time advocating for people to just chill out a little bit and enjoy the ride. Look, last night was great. The Spurs took over the lead for the last time at the end of the 1st quarter, and it never really felt like they were challenged after that. The Pelicans got within six points of them with about four minutes left in the 2nd half, and then Wemby slammed the door on them so hard that you could almost hear metaphorical hinges rattle. The Spurs were up by thirteen in roughly a minute-and-a-half, and that was that. They spent most of the 2nd half up by 20+ plus points, and Wemby sat with six minutes left in the fourth, after absolutely drilling a pair of threes to crush what little spirit the Pelicans had remaining, and get to that nice round number of fifty points. And all I could think was: “What the hell am I supposed to write about this?” I know. Victor Wembanyama dropped his 2nd Wilt Chamberlain stat-line of the last couple weeks, and all I could think about was how hard he was making it for me to write about the game. That’s how spoiled I am already. I sat through the years of losing, and bellyached about that, and now I’ve got find something else to bellyache about again, I guess. And don’t get me wrong, finding new ways to write about 18 and 16 game losing streaks isn’t easy either, but when everything is going wrong, it isn’t hard to assess the situation. At that point, it’s mostly just a matter of honing in on your favorite disasters and picking at the scab. But a game like this from Wemby is a tide that raises all boats. Are the Spurs are as good they looked last night? Maybe not. But it’s an impenetrable maybe, because they haven’t been shooting well, and they’re missing players, and it still looked like child’s play. Is that because Wemby is currently performing like the greatest historical outlier since the 60’s, or does this team have a ceiling that none of us could reasonably conceive of? Consider that Julian Champagnie and Harrison Barnes went a combined 4-17 last night. Maybe I could focus in on that on another evening, but it gets lost in the onslaught, because how do you complain about that on a night that the Spurs beat a team by 23 points? How can I reasonably critique that the Spurs didn’t beat the Pelicans by 40 points instead? I might as well complain that Wemby didn’t stay in for the final six minutes to put up 60 points. It’s not even an embarrassment of riches at that point. I’d feel like a nepo-baby complaining about the limitations of their trust fund. Who wants to listen to me piss and moan about Luke Kornet being a -11 on the night, or De’Aaron Fox only scoring 5 points and taking just four shots but still tallying 10 assists and being 2nd on the team in plus-minus (+33)? How do I even access that kind of cynicism after watching Wemby levitate and undulate, like a colossal squid plucking fish out of the depths, at the behest of his basketball-loving whims. Do I focus on the defense? There were flaws, to be sure, but the bench held up their end of the deal for once and won their minutes. Was that sustainable, or just a part of the magic? I honestly couldn’t tell you. The last time Wemby went for 50 they had no such luck. It’s a lot easier to find something to harp on when you only win by a single point. Earlier this week a prominent mathematician with a track record for solving ‘unsolvable’ mathematics problems with the help of AI, announced a proof of one of the 7 Millennium Prize Problems (The Riemann hypothesis). And all I could do was sit there and wonder (supposing it holds up) how much of the problem had been solved by him, and how much had been solved by AI? That’s what writing about these kinds of Wemby games feels like. It’s like he’s out there solving basketball’s millennium prize problems, and we’re all sitting there wondering how much his teammates actually contributed to it. I guess it doesn’t really matter in the end. He’s solving problems no one else can, and we’re all just along for the ride. It’s crazy to be at the point where it feels so normal that I’m able to even focus on anything else at all. It’s a good problem to have. I hope I never have to solve it. Takeaways Carter Bryant continues to confound me. I certainly can’t complain that he didn’t get enough playing time in this one, as he and Barnes got about 20 minutes each, but I can’t remember the last time I was as confounded by a player’s defense as his. There are moment where he looks like he could end up being the 2nd best perimeter defender on the team, and moments where he looks every bit as confused as he did as a rookie. We know he can hold his own for short stretches having seen it last postseason, but the closest comparison I can think of for his confusing moments of hesitancy is the way that one-time Spur Lonnie Walker used to inexplicably lose all confidence on the offensive end. I’m still looking for it to click for Carter (who, admittedly, hasn’t gotten a lot of time to work on it), but I’m worried that (as with Lonnie) it never truly will. It was nice to see Mitch Johnson actually do the thing and give Tarris Reed some run even though Kornet only saw the court for 10 minutes. I did not expect to see Reed jack up a three, at all. But it does make me wonder if they’re working on that with him. One of the real difficulties both units seem to have is adjusting to Kornet’s limitations when Wemby’s not on the court. But if Reed could assume some facsimile of a backup stretch big, that could yield significant rewards in the future. At the very least, I like that he has the confidence to let it fly. I feel like the bodes well in other ways too. I honestly can’t beleive that I’m typing this, but if the Spurs remain committed to playing their best guards together, they might need to think about picking up another guard in the next draft. As much as I like Jordan McLaughlin and David Jones Garcia, they’re really more suited to serve as two-guards over leading the offense. MATFO working their late-draft guard voodoo to find themselves another Cory Joseph would be the icing on an already terrifyingly tiered cake. teamStories.summary: Victor Wembanyama had his third career 50-point outing during a win over the Pelicans to go along with 19 rebounds, five blocks and four steals.
teamStories.detailText: SAN ANTONIO -- Victor Wembanyama overwhelmed the New Orleans Pelicans with his third career 50-point outing Saturday, when he also became the first player in the play-by-play era to tally at least 30 points, 10 rebounds, three blocks and three steals in a half, to lead the San Antonio Spurs to a 114-91 win . Wembanyama had 32 points, 12 rebounds, three steals and three blocked shots in the first half, a stat line no other player has matched in an entire game this season. He did that in nearly 18 minutes as the Spurs sent the Pelicans to their ninth loss in 10 games. The 22-year-old finished with 19 rebounds, five blocks and four steals and admitted to some stat padding after Spurs coach Mitch Johnson told him he had 1:30 left of playing time to reach 50 points. "I told him it might be enough [time]," Wembanyama said. He was correct. In 1:14 of the fourth quarter, Wembanyama drilled back-to-back 3-pointers to reach 50 points and give San Antonio a 108-82 lead. Wembanyama took a seat on the Spurs' bench between Luke Kornet and De'Aaron Fox 22 seconds later, when Johnson called a timeout to sub him out for rookie Tarris Reed Jr. "I just want to keep stacking them up," Wembanyama said of his historic performances. "I don't plan on doing those. They just come when we play the right way as a team. Hopefully, there's many more coming." Wembanyama tied LeBron James and Devin Booker for the second-most 50-point performances in NBA history by a player 22 or younger. Wembanyama joined Hall of Famer and former Spurs great David Robinson as the only players with multiple 50-point, five-block games in league history since blocks were tracked (1973-74). Wembanyama is the first player to do it multiple times in the same season. "He started the game off aggressive, and he was trying to play with a lot of force offensively, specifically in terms of taking up real estate, trying to get to the rim," Johnson said. "It's so interesting when people play like that, especially with his talent level. Then, it helps your rhythm with your shots and everything else. I was just hoping he got to 50 when he did. That would've been hard to take him out that close to 50." Wembanyama notched his second career half with at least 30 points with near surgical precision. He hit 12 of 15 shots from the field, including 3 of 5 from 3-point range over the first two quarters. With 2:30 remaining until intermission, Wembanyama had outscored New Orleans' starting five. Reigning NBA Sixth Man of the Year Keldon Johnson perused the box score during the postgame news conference, taking in what he had just witnessed. With his eyes darting back and forth, Johnson started to rattle off Wembanyama's numbers. "Vic had 50 tonight. That was impressive. [He shot] 20-for-29; that's crazy," Johnson said. "He had it rolling, and the main thing was if he's open or getting to his spots, make sure you give it to him. That's just the emphasis for everybody." Actress and singer Selena Gomez sat courtside among the sellout crowd of 18,708 at Frost Bank Center, and Wembanyama made sure the longtime Spurs fan was entertained. Wembanyama glanced at Gomez in the first half to acknowledge her presence after he knocked down a corner 3. "Of course," Wembanyama said, laughing. "I had to show out for Selena." He even acknowledged postgame that the "ethical basketball" he espoused last season wasn't part of the equation or thought process at the end of a career night in which he forced up one last 3-pointer. "Ethical basketball, there's not really a clearly defined term what it means," he said. "But for me, what it means is creating a culture as a team, taking the right shots, beating teams by having everybody on the floor as a threat for the opponent at all times. That step-back [3] to the right I took, it doesn't correlate with this. It didn't fit to the definition. Yeah, I did try to get a 3 up when I had 47 points." Was he OK with breaking from the tenets he defines as ethical basketball? "Yeah, of course," he said. "I made it, didn't I? I don't think Wilt [Chamberlain] thought about [stat padding] when he had 98 points. I don't think he thought about making the extra, extra pass. If he could've went for 100, he would've, and he did. I try to not think about it."

teamStories.summary: San Antonio Spurs star Victor Wembanyama hits 50 points as his side beats the New Orleans Pelicans 114-91.
teamStories.detailText: Victor Wembanyama was selected by the San Antonio Spurs with the first overall pick in the 2023 NBA draft. [Reuters] San Antonio Spurs star Victor Wembanyama hit 50 points in a historic performance as his side beat the New Orleans Pelicans 114-91. The 22-year-old, who is 7ft 4ins tall, became the first player with 50 points, five blocks and five three-pointers in a match since the NBA added threes in 1979–80. The France international, who was defensive player of the year for 2026, said he put on a show for a celebrity-packed crowd which included actress and long-time Spurs fan Selena Gomez. "I had to show off for Selena," he said. "I just want to keep stacking them [records] up. I don't plan on doing those. They just come and we play the right way as a team. "So, I just want to stack them up. Hopefully there's many more coming." The Spurs have made a fine start to the season, winning 14 of their 17 games so far to top the Western Conference Southwest. They won the division last season before losing to the New York Knicks in the NBA Finals. Spurs coach Mitch Johnson added. "It's a cliche to say, 'Why doesn't he do it every game?' "But it's so interesting when people play like that, especially with his talent." 'I'm not very good at stat-padding' Wembanyama's haul - the third of his career - came after James Harden scored 51 points to move third on the all-time list for 50-point NBA games on Saturday. Wilt Chamberlain holds the record with an incredible 118 50-point games. "It is very special. But unlike many of my peers, I'm not very good at stat-padding," Wembanyama said. "So I haven't reached it as many times as I should have." Wembanyama was later asked whether there was an ethical right or wrong way to score 50 points. Some NBA players have been accused of chasing individual statistics for financial gain instead of concentrating on their team's results. "Maybe, I think that's a question for you. The greats, they don't think about that," Wembanyama replied. "I don't think LeBron [James], Shai [Gilgeous-Alexander], [Nikola] Jokic, [Luka] Doncic, I don't think they think about that. I have them as examples, so I'm trying to not think about it either."

teamStories.detailText: SAN ANTONIO, TX - NOVEMBER 21: Victor Wembanyama #1 of the San Antonio Spurs reaches for a rebound against Zion Williamson #1 of the New Orleans Pelicans in the first half at Frost Bank Center on November 21, 2026 in San Antonio, Texas. (Photo by Ronald Cortes/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Antonio Spurs closed out their three-game homestand with a 114-91 victory over the New Orleans Pelicans at the Frost Bank Center on Saturday night in front of a sold out crowd, which included one very special celebrity guest, singer and actress Selena Gomez. Victor Wembanyama posted 50 points, 18 rebounds, 5 three-pointers, and 5 blocks in 32 minutes. At one point during the first half, Wembanyama hit one of his five threes on the night, turned towards the crowd and smiled in Gomez’s direction. “I had to show off for Selena (Gomez),” he said, smiling as he answered. Wembanyama came out aggressive from the opening tip, scoring 17 of the Spurs’ 32 points in the opening quarter. He went to rim for dunks, hit free throws, and scored from the mid range. San Antonio had 30 assists on the night and 14 of those were off a made Wemby basket. Nothing New Orleans did worked on this night to stop the Spurs’ French star from accomplishing his goal of scoring 50 points, no matter how hard they tried. Pelicans coach Jamahl Mosley doubled Wembanyama with multiple players, but the Spurs’ forward backed down the smaller player right into the paint or when he was triple teamed, he found Julian Champagnie or Devin Vassell for an open three. “I thought he started the game off aggressive,” Spurs Head Coach Mitch Johnson said of Wembanyama after the game. “It’s so interesting when people play like that, especially with his talent and then it helps with your shots. I thought he did a really good job of playing with force.” Despite Wembanyama’s great night, Johnson still had a criticism for his star player and that is his passing. Late in the half, Wemby secured a defensive rebound and brought the ball up court. Instead of finding the open Keldon Johnson, the French star pulled up for three and missed, ignoring his open teammate. “Keldon has to have the ball in that moment,” Mitch Johnson said. “When you play the right way, things like that happen.” As good as the Spurs looked on Saturday, they still struggled in the non-Wemby minutes. New Orleans outscored the Spurs 22-13 in the first half when Wembanyama sat, but things were even when he sat in the second half. The reason? Johnson put in Luke Kornet, Harrison Barnes, and Carter Bryant. However, he kept Devin Vassell and Stephon Castle on the floor with that second unit. “I thought we had some moments where we did a really good job defensively in terms of shrinking the floor and showing crowds and gang rebounding,” Mitch Johnson said. “That group, probably, the worst minutes of the non Victor, has nothing to do with Luke, in my opinion. It’s when we take quick shots, and then we’re in transition defense a lot, and we’re on our heels.” As a result of those lineup changes, Castle turned it on and scored 19 points on the night to go along with six assists. “It’s been reflective ever since he’s been on this team,” Wembanayama said of Castle. “He’s been impactful in a meaningful way and he’s impacted winning ever since he arrived here.” Game Notes: Keldon Johnson had 10 points off the bench, scoring in double figures for the fourth time in the last five games. If he can continue to deliver at that level consistently, the bench unit will be much improved as the season goes on. “When I do the right things on the court, the scoring will come,” Keldon said after the game. De’Aaron Fox slipped on a wet spot on the floor during the first half and was limping a bit before being taken out of the game. He would return later and Mitch Johnson said after the game that Fox was fine. Still, Fox scored just 5 points on 1-for-4 shooting and one has to wonder if his hip injury is bothering him. Up Next: The Spurs are now 14-3 on the season and will return to the court on Monday night when they face the Sacramento Kings at 9 p.m.

stories.title: 'Locked into the moment,' Bryce Young rallies first-place Panthers past Ravens
stories.summary: In a back-and-forth game laced with lead changes, Bryce Young rallied the Panthers to a 35-33 home win over the Baltimore Ravens on Sunday at Bank of America Stadium, a second straight victory for the 5-5 Panthers that padded lead in the NFC South.
stories.detailText: CHARLOTTE, N.C. -- With the game on the line, Carolina Panthers coach Dave Canales wants quarterback Bryce Young in the driver's seat. And the fourth-year QB -- whom Canales benched in 2024 -- showed exactly why he's earned that trust from his boss in a 35-33 come-from-behind home win over the Baltimore Ravens (4-7) on Sunday at Bank of America Stadium. Young drove the Panthers' offense 55 yards down the field to set up a game-winning 37-yard field goal for kicker Ryan Fitzgerald with 1:44 left in the fourth quarter. After the ball flew through the uprights, Young ultimately produced the 14th game-winning drive of his career and the fifth win of Carolina's up-and-down season. "Game on the line, there's nobody else I want with the ball," Canales said. "Bryce Young is going to go there, he's going to be in control, he's going to be focused and locked into the moment, and that's what he looked like on that drive." Canales and Young have come a long way since 2024 when the then-second-year QB was shelved for backup Andy Dalton ahead of the coach's third-ever regular-season game. Young returned to the lineup after being benched for five games, and he hasn't really looked back since. Last season, Young and Canales led the Panthers to their first NFC South title -- albeit at 8-9 -- since 2015. This season, with Canales handing over offensive playcalling to coordinator Brad Idzik, Young is on pace for career highs in most major passing categories. Against Baltimore, Young led six scoring drives, as he produced 254 passing yards, two touchdowns and an interception. The Panthers and Ravens traded leads seven times, and Young -- with the backing of Canales -- put the exclamation point on the back-and-forth battle with a balanced field-goal drive. After Canales declared his trust in Young, the QB acknowledged the statement from his coach was important to him. "Yeah, it means a lot," Young said about Canales' postgame statement. "Obviously, everything that I want to do, us as a unit, we want to go out and do is to have his back and protect him out on the field. We talk about it all the time. When we're out there, whoever is carrying the ball, you carry the hopes and dreams of the organization, everything like that. In those moments, I trust the guys around me. "We all kind of rally off of each other, so again, I'm super proud of the guys, finding a way down there to get three [points], and then our defense, finishing it on our terms. Them getting a turnover in a game like that, it's huge. It's a team effort, but yeah, it definitely means a lot." The Panthers (5-5) are two games ahead of the rest of the NFC South heading into Week 12. They'll travel to face division rival, the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-7), on "Monday Night Football." A lot has changed -- most notably the Panthers' defensive coordinator, from Ejiro Evero to Todd Wash -- since the Buccaneers blew out the Panthers 43-13 on their home turf in Week 7. So, the Panthers might need to count on Young's clutch nature again in short order. For what it's worth, team captain and defensive tackle Derrick Brown says watching Young lead game-winning drives never gets old. "Hell no," Brown said. "The goal is to win [laughs], so I'm not going to apologize to no damn body for f---ing how we win. If it takes until the last second, that's what it is."

stories.title: Tyler Shough voices confidence in Saints, Kellen Moore after 3-7 start
stories.summary: Two straight losses. Justin Reid being released. Run game a mess. Despite the challenges, there's belief New Orleans can turn things around.
stories.detailText: CHICAGO -- It has been a month of turmoil for the New Orleans Saints and quarterback Tyler Shough . The Saints fell to 3-7 on Sunday after a 21-13 loss to the Chicago Bears , a loss that effectively seals their postseason fate unless they find a way to run the table in their final seven games. With the Cincinnati Bengals and their top-ranked passing offense up next in Week 12, that will be a tall task. Beyond Sunday's loss, team captain Justin Reid asked for, and was granted his release just last week. There have been injuries to the offensive line and kicking issues have persisted despite a change this month. The Saints fired run game coordinator T.J. Paganetti , but the starting quarterback remains the team's leading rusher. Despite the seven losses, Shough said he still believes New Orleans is a good team. The QB noted the Saints have been in every game except the Week 4 loss to the Atlanta Falcons . Right now, Shough says it's "a great opportunity for myself and everybody to look in the mirror and understand how bad [they] really want this." He admitted it's not going to be easy. "Even the great teams that go through these storms find a way to continue to go through it. And that's all it is right now," Shough said. "... Every single week you work six, seven days a week all day. Our mood, our result, is dependent on that one outcome, but you can't let it derail it and obviously you have to let it fuel you, but I know I'm going to be better because of these moments and our team is going to be as well." Shough, who made his 19th start in Chicago, has had his share of those moments in the past three games. Some of it was out of his control, but others have been a result of poor decision-making. The second-year QB has been playing with broken bones in his non-throwing hand and wore a glove until Sunday, noting that the injury has been "healing." He completed 25 of 42 passes for 222 yards, threw an interception that the Bears turned into a touchdown, and was sacked six times, including one that resulted in a safety. Shough has now been sacked 14 times in the past three games behind an offensive line missing center Erik McCoy and right tackle Taliese Fuaga . The sacks have been a mixture of protection issues from his teammates and Shough's own mistakes -- whether he was holding the ball too long or attempting to take off and run. The safety, which occurred early in the fourth quarter on second-and-10, was both. Coach Kellen Moore said that wide receiver Jordyn Tyson was supposed to help in protection on the play. "We should be helping the right tackle on that play, and obviously, we just didn't execute it. So the edge rusher had the angle," Moore said. Bears defensive lineman Montez Sweat beat Mason Murphy on Shough's right side to sack him. "Got off Cover 2 and I was working through my progression, [trying to] find the shallow and it progressed to another read," Shough said. "They matched some of it out, but we're expecting a chip on the right side ... obviously crucial one there and just sucks. But in retrospect, I could have stepped up earlier to the run, but it's hard, expecting some presence there, but he did a good job. So just unfortunate." Shough was asked about the team's confidence in Moore after a game where the Saints made the same mistakes they've made since last season -- namely slow starts and turnovers. He cited the close games again, saying Moore has had a good game plan every week. "We've lost by a score or less on every single one of our losses other than one where it got kind of out of our hands quickly there, but it's come down to a couple plays," Shough said. "So ultimately we have to find a way to figure out what that issue is. But I think more than anything, Kellen's done a good job. I love working with Kellen. I mean, it's not going to be perfect by no means, but we all are riding together."

stories.title: Bills' Grand Theft Auto VI-themed jab at Dolphins tops NFL Week 11 trolls
stories.summary: NFL teams remained petty in Week 11, led by a petty post from the Buffalo Bills.
stories.detailText: Grand Theft Auto VI has taken over the entertainment world since its release last Thursday. The video game's reach carried over to the NFL, too, becoming the theme of a petty post on Sunday. The Buffalo Bills defeated the Miami Dolphins 26-9 led by its defense. Buffalo allowed just 185 yards and picked off Dolphins quarterback Kyle McCord once. Josh Allen had two interceptions himself, but he also threw for 304 yards and a score. Other teams such as the New York Jets and Chicago Bears tapped into the GTA VI space, but the Bills' attempt felt more direct as they faced the Dolphins. The victory prompted Buffalo to post a custom game cover inspired by that of GTA VI, which is set in "Vice City," a fictional version of Miami. Instead of it reading "GTA VI" across the cover, the Bills added: "Bills Win" with players scattered throughout it. Here are the top trolls from NFL's Week 11. Carolina Panthers 35, Baltimore Ravens 33 It required a late stop, but the Carolina Panthers pulled out a wild victory against the Baltimore Ravens . Carolina went ahead with a 37-yard field goal as 1:44 remained in the game. Baltimore received possession with a chance to go ahead for good before Jacoby Brissett was picked off with 36 ticks left, clinching the Panthers' win. A clever caption kicked off Carolina's trolling as it wrote: "came down to the wire," with "the wire" being a reference to the iconic HBO show set in Baltimore. Then, the Panthers shared a graphic of a panther standing over a Ravens helmet with the caption: "Charming," a reference to Baltimore's nickname as the "Charm City." They also wrote "nevermore" on the bottom in a nod to Edgar Allen Poe's "The Raven" poem where the raven featured repeats: "nevermore." Dallas Cowboys 50, Tennessee Titans 31 A 50-burger wasn't enough for the Dallas Cowboys , who rubbed salt in the Tennessee Titans ' wounds postgame. Dallas scored a touchdown on its first six possessions, the first time that has happened in franchise history since at least 1978, according to ESPN Research. Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott provided five of the team's seven touchdowns -- four in the air and one on the ground. Texas and Tennessee are known for their rich histories in country music, but the Cowboys claimed superiority over the Titans by captioning their post: "Texas Country," which has its unique sound. Philadelphia Eagles 19, Pittsburgh Steelers 16 The Philadelphia Eagles held on to defeat the Pittsburgh Steelers at home, snapping a seven-game winless streak. Philadelphia put up 13 points in the first quarter, pacing it the rest of the game as Pittsburgh's offense struggled. The Steelers finally found the endzone with 1:20 left in the fourth, but it was too little, too late. They couldn't stop the Eagles on their ensuing drive and Philadelphia survived to win. Held at Lincoln Financial Field, it was an in-state matchup between Pennsylvania's two squads. The Eagles claimed Pennsylvania with a postgame caption that read: "Our State" on an image of linebacker Jalyx Hunt pointing to the sky and Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers in the background.
